Former Legislative Council member Wong Kam-fai has been charged with dangerous driving and other offences and is currently on bail pending trial. He served as a member from December 2022 to July this year. According to Legislative Council records reviewed by Chi Koi Se (集誌社), Wong's office incurred total operating expenses exceeding $10 million during his more than 42-month term, including over $1.5 million in consultancy fees. He successively hired Chan Tak-ming, president of the "Hong Kong Guangzhou Innovation and Technology Association" he founded, and vice president Ng Hok-ling, as consultants. Chan Tak-ming has been continuously engaged since January 2023, receiving $20,000 to $30,000 per month, totalling over $1 million in consultancy fees. According to the guidelines for Legislative Council members' application for reimbursement of working expenses, "a member should not engage as consultants any company or organisation in which his political party or any organisation controlled by his party has a financial interest." Is there an issue with hiring key members of related organisations as paid consultants? The Legislative Council Secretariat, in response to Chi Koi Se's enquiry, stated that the guidelines have been set out and no further comments would be made. Wong, who has no political affiliations, responded that the association operates on a voluntary basis as a non-profit. Additionally, at the tail end of his first term, Wong also distributed bonuses to office staff, with total staff expenses of over $773,000 claimed from the Legislative Council that month.

Office operating expenses exceeding $10 million during his term

Chi Koi Se reviewed Wong Kam-fai's "reimbursement amounts for office operating expenses" in the Seventh Legislative Council, ranging from approximately $2.877 million to $2.984 million per year; from October 2025, in the Eighth Legislative Council, the amount was raised to $3.02 million. During his 42-month term, Wong claimed total office operating expenses exceeding $10 million from the Legislative Council. In 2023 and 2024, his claimed expenses were approximately $1.876 million and $2.89 million respectively.

However, in 2025, Wong's claimed expenses amounted to $4.006 million. Reasons for the increase include: staff expenses rose from $2.24 million the previous year to $3.215 million; consultancy fees also increased from $480,000 to $640,000. After Wong was re-elected in 2026, expenses from January to June totalled $1.413 million.

Spending over $1 million to hire senior executives of his own association as legislative consultants

According to records, from February 2023 to June 2026, Wong claimed over $1.5 million in consultancy fees from the Legislative Council. Of this, during the 36 months from 2023 to 2025, he continuously engaged Chan Tak-ming, president of the "Hong Kong Guangzhou Innovation and Technology Association," at $30,000 per month, spending $1.08 million. After Wong was re-elected this term and until his resignation, within six months, he continued to engage Chan Tak-ming at $20,000 per month, spending $120,000 in total. The "Hong Kong Guangzhou Innovation and Technology Association" was founded by Wong Kam-fai in 2016, with Wong serving as executive president.

Three consultancy tenders, two bidders are members of the "Association"

As early as March 2023, Wong submitted tender documents to the Legislative Council, with three consultancy bids from Tai Ching-fung, Chan Tak-ming, and Cheng Kwok-wai. Both Tai and Chan were members of the "Hong Kong Guangzhou Innovation and Technology Association," with Tai serving as head of the finance group. Tai bid $45,000, Cheng bid $35,000, and Chan's bid was the lowest at $30,000; ultimately Chan secured the consultancy work.

The tender document stated that Chan's consultancy work involved assisting in advocacy and planning for innovation and technology, education, various social policies and issues; facilitating interaction and communication across sectors; and supporting regional office operations.

Hiring the Association's vice president as consultant with only one bid

Wong also engaged association vice president Ng Hok-ling as a consultant. From June 2023 onwards, Ng Hok-ling served Wong as a consultant on innovation and technology and education policy matters, receiving $5,000 in consultancy fees for the first month, then $10,000 per month thereafter, totalling $315,000. Ng Hok-ling's consultancy work had only one bid. Regarding the scope of work in the tender, Wong stated that Ng was "proficient in both innovation and technology and education policies," "able to respond quickly to work requirements with flexible service arrangements, and the service quality meets the needs of my parliamentary work."

Legislative Council guidelines: should not engage organisations controlled by political parties as consultants

According to section 24 of the Legislative Council's "Guidelines for Members' Application for Reimbursement of Working Expenses," "a member should not engage as consultants any company/organisation in which his/her political party or any company/organisation having a financial interest in or control by his/her political party." Wong Kam-fai, who has no political affiliations: The Association operates on a non-profit basis

Chi Koi Se enquired with Wong Kam-fai whether hiring key members of related organisations as consultants might conflict with the guidelines. Wong replied that Chan Tak-ming handled district and political liaison matters, while Ng Hok-ling covered the education field. Wong stated that the association was co-founded by a group of like-minded innovation and technology professionals who hoped to contribute to Hong Kong and mainland China's innovation and technology development, saying "we all work on a voluntary basis and have always operated as a non-profit." Records show that Wong has no political affiliations.

Office director received $276,000 in salary upon contract completion

Regarding consultancy expenses, in terms of remuneration for legislative assistants, records show that when Wong completed his term in 2025, he claimed two staff expense items totalling over $773,000 from the Legislative Council, of which approximately $423,000 was for paid leave, together with salaries for November and December.

Wong also distributed approximately $350,000 in bonuses to five office staff members, among whom Wong's office director had a monthly salary of $63,500. Upon completion of the term in December, she received paid annual leave compensation, together with two months' salary totalling approximately $181,000, plus a bonus equivalent to 1.5 months' salary of $95,200, totalling $276,000. The other four staff members received bonuses from Wong equivalent to 2.5 months' salary, ranging from $54,000 to $75,000 each.

Legislative Council Secretariat: Reimbursement guidelines have been set out

Chi Koi Se previously enquired with the Legislative Council Secretariat regarding the appropriateness of Wong's practices of hiring his association's president and vice president as long-term consultants and distributing bonuses. The Secretariat responded that the relevant details have been set out in the guidelines for Legislative Council members' application for reimbursement of working expenses and no further comments would be made.

Selected guiding principles of the "Guidelines for Legislative Council Members' Application for Reimbursement of Working Expenses": · Members or their relatives should not have any direct or indirect financial interest in transactions involving reimbursement applications. · Members should avoid applying for reimbursement for any transaction that might lead the public to believe that the member themselves, their relatives, or business partners could benefit. · Members should adhere to the principles of openness, fairness, and accountability when using public funds. · Where conflicts of interest cannot be avoided or have arisen, members should declare such interests when applying for reimbursement, with declarations being available for public inspection. · If transactions for which reimbursement is being or may be applied for give rise to suspicion of conflicts of interest... members should handle such matters with the principle of public interest as the priority. · Members should, as far as possible, separate their private affairs/interests from those of the Legislative Council, and make it known to the public that they have done so, in order to avoid suspicion of conflicts of interest or improper personal gain.

Guidelines for Legislative Council Members' Use of Consultancy Services: Members may engage consultants on a standing or ad hoc basis... to avoid conflicts of interest, the following requirements must be met: · Individual contracts should be signed with each engaged consultant · Contracts should clearly specify the scope of services provided by the consultant · The names of consultants and fees charged should be listed on reimbursement claim documents for public inspection · A copy of the contract should be submitted to the Secretariat (contracts are not required to be made available for public inspection) · Members or their relatives should not have any interest relationship with engaged consultants · Members should not engage as consultants any company/organisation in which their political party or any organisation having a financial interest in or control by their political party

In the declaration records, Wong Kam-fai categorised the bonus amounts as "other," stating that no bonuses had been distributed during the first three years of the term and that the arrangement was discretionary, "therefore not specified in the contract." He also stated that the team had assisted in promoting and implementing various bills, motions, and initiatives, and that "after careful consideration of the office's financial situation, I have decided to award bonuses to the following staff members in recognition of their diligent efforts and contributions during the Seventh Legislative Council term." According to the "Guidelines for Application for Reimbursement of Working Expenses," members may set aside funds from the reimbursement amount for office operating expenses to pay for staff contract bonuses, double pay, or end-of-contract gratuities. The amount set aside should be based on contracts signed between both parties and other legal obligations, and should not be excessive; members may receive payment without submitting supporting documents.

On 29 June this year, Wong Kam-fai was suspected of hitting two vehicles within the Chinese University campus and fleeing the scene, and was arrested by police on four charges including suspected drink driving and careless driving. On 1 July, the media exposed Wong's involvement in the case before he had declared it to the Legislative Council, and he attended the Reunification Day reception as usual for photo opportunities. It was not until 3 July that Wong resigned from all positions in the Legislative Council.

Apart from being a member of the Election Committee constituency in the Legislative Council, Wong is also a member of the 14th National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, and Associate Dean (External Affairs) of the Faculty of Engineering at CUHK. Following the drink driving incident, CUHK announced the suspension of his administrative duties to date. In September this year, police formally charged him with four offences including "dangerous driving," and he was granted bail. The case has been adjourned to 11 November for mention.
